【 CASE REPORT 】
Disappearance of Hepatocellular Adenoma in a Patient with
Cornelia de Lange Syndrome after Treatment with
Transcatheter Arterial Embolization
Kazuhide Takata 1, Takanori Kitaguchi 1, Hiroaki Tokushige 1, Takahiro Nagata 1,
Takashi Miyayama 1, Kumiko Shibata 1, Hiromi Fukuda 1, Ryo Yamauchi 1, Atsushi Fukunaga 1,
Takashi Tanaka 1
, Keiji Yokoyama 1, Satoshi Shakado1, Kengo Yoshimitsu2, Hironori Kusano 3,
Shotaro Sakisaka 1 and Fumihito Hirai 1
Abstract:
Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a congenital disorder occasionally associated with congenital portosystemic shunt (CPSS). We herein report a patient with CdLS and CPSS who developed hepatocellular adenomas (HCAs). The patient presented to our hospital for the further investigation of newly diagnosed liver tumors. Imaging findings and pathological examination results indicated that the liver tumors were inflammatory HCAs that subsequently shrank following transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE). Patients with CdLS
and CPSS are at risk of developing HCAs, and TAE may be an effective management strategy for HCA in
these patients.
Key words: hepatocellular adenoma, transcatheter arterial embolization, TAE, Cornelia de Lange syndrome
(Intern Med 63: 1569-1573, 2024)
(DOI: 10.2169/internalmedicine.2537-23)
Introduction
Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a multisystem genetic disorder with an incidence of 1 per 10,000-30,000 live
births. The characteristics of CdLS include pre- and postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, facial dysmorphia, developmental delay, intellectual disabilities, hirsutism, limb

malformations, and small hands and feet, as well as cardiac,
gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and vascular anomalies (1, 2).
Liver tumors such as hepatocellular adenomas (HCAs)
frequently occur in patients with CdLS (3). However, its
pathological mechanisms and management remain unknown.
We herein report a 20-year-old woman with CdLS who
developed concurrent HCAs that were successfully treated
with transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE).
Case Report
A 20-year-old woman presented to our hospital for the
further investigation of newly observed liver tumors that
were not detected on imaging examinations 6 years prior to
presentation. The patient had been diagnosed with CdLS at
birth and had undergone tracheostomy at 19 years old for
repeated aspiration pneumonia triggered by gastroesophageal
reflux. The patient had no history of alcohol consumption or
the use of oral contraceptives or other steroidal medications.
The patient’s vital signs were stable, and her weight and
height were 23.5 kg and 131 cm, respectively. A physical
examination revealed facial features consistent with CdLS,
including thick eyebrows, a depressed nasal bridge, an anteriorly tilted nose, a flat palate, and a thin upper lip, as well
as developmental delays, intellectual disabilities, a missing
right IV finger, and syndactyly of the right I and II toes.

Laboratory tests revealed elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase levels and a decreased platelet count. All tumor markers were within the normal ranges (Table).
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed
38-mm and 19-mm nodules in the sixth segment (S6) and
first segment (S1) of the liver, respectively. On CT, these
nodules demonstrated enhancement during the early phase
and hypodensity during the late phase (Fig. 1a-d). In addition, intrahepatic portal vein stenosis with predominant involvement in the left lobe, marked splenomegaly, a massive
gastrorenal shunt suggestive of portal hypertension, and duplicated inferior vena cava were observed. Gadolinium
ethoxybenzyl-diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid-enhanced
magnetic resonance imaging with hepatobiliary phase and

fat-suppressed T2-weighted images showed diffusely increased intensity in the S6 tumor and ring-shaped increased
intensity - a characteristic known as the “atoll sign” seen in
inflammatory hepatocellular adenoma - in the S1 tumor
(Fig. 1e-h) (4).
A histological examination of percutaneous liver tumor
biopsy specimens obtained from the S1 and S6 tumors revealed slightly higher cellularity of hepatocytes in the tumor
tissue than in the surrounding tissue, with sinusoidal dilatation and unpaired arteries. The hepatocytes exhibited round
nuclei of mildly irregular size and mild cellular atypia
(Fig. 2a, b). In addition, the tumors showed epithelial granulomas and arterial wall muscle thickening (Fig. 2c, d).
CD34+α-SMA double immunostaining revealed capillarization of sinusoids in the tumors. The tumors also showed
positive expression for C-reactive protein and serum amyloid
A. Gultamine synthetase was focally positive, and hepatic
fatty acid-binding protein (L-FABP) was preserved. There
was no nuclear expression of β-catenin in the tumor cells
(Fig. 2e-k). Based on the imaging, pathological, and immunohistological findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory HCAs associated with abnormal intrahepatic
blood flow.
Subsequent surveillance revealed substantial tumor enlargement. Regarding the S6 lesion, the tumor was large (>5
cm) widely abutting the liver surface, and a risk of rupture
was suggested; however, hepatic resection was considered
unfeasible because of the patient’s condition. Therefore, 18
months after the initial diagnosis, TAE was performed under
general anesthesia for the S6 tumor alone via the A6 feeding
artery using gelatin sponge fragments under general anesthesia (Fig. 3). The intervention proved to be effective and resulted in a persistent volume reduction of both the treated
S6 tumor and the untreated S1 tumor over the subsequent
five years (Fig. 4).
Discussion
The present patient’s clinical presentation had two important clinical implications.
First, patients with concomitant CdLS and portal vein

(PV) hypoplasia can develop liver tumors. PV hypoplasia in
the present case resulted in portal hypertension, manifesting
as a gastro-renal shunt between the portal venous system
and the systemic venous circulation. The patient presented
with multiple liver tumors and imaging findings suggestive
of HCAs (5). HCAs are benign liver tumors with multiple
subtypes, and their diagnosis requires pathological and immunohistological examinations (6). In this case, these examinations indicated that the liver tumors were inflammatory HCAs. Congenital portosystemic shunt (CPSS), along
with PV hypoplasia, is a vascular malformation that can
cause hepatic encephalopathy, pulmonary hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome, and liver tumors due to intrahepatic blood flow imbalance. Baiges et al. reported that 18 of
66 patients with congenital extrahepatic portosystemic
shunts had neoplastic lesions (8 HCCs and 10 adenomas),
and 25 patients had non-neoplastic nodules (7 nodular regenerative hyperplasia, 12 focal nodular hyperplasia, and 6
non-specific nodules) (7). This association has been suggested to be related to the absence of or decrease in portal
venous flow, which leads to compensatory arterial hyperperfusion and formation of regenerative/hyperplastic nodules.

described a case of CdLS-associated liver tumors suspected
to be hyperplastic nodules or hepatoblastomas on a pathological examination (3). Therefore, patients with CdLS and
CPSS require monitoring for the development of liver tumors.

Second, TAE is a safe and effective treatment for CPSSinduced HCAs. Hepatic resection is the standard treatment
for patients with an HCA >5 cm to avoid the risk of hemorrhaging and malignant transformation (8). However, liver resection of unruptured benign tumors is associated with a
morbidity rate of up to 7.2% (9). TAE was selected as a
low-invasiveness treatment because of the presence of multiple intrahepatic HCA nodules and the patient’s general condition due to various malformations; its effects were sustained for over five years. Extensive intrahepatic embolization in patients with CPSS may result in postoperative liver
failure due to hepatic infarction, similar to TAE in patients
with complete portal vein obstruction. However, in our patient, selective embolization of the S6 target nodule was
safely performed because portal vein angiography confirmed
that the portal vein in the right lobe of the liver was secure.
van Rosmalen et al. reported the efficacy and safety of TAE
for the treatment of HCAs (10). In our case, it was demonstrated that HCAs induced by CPSS could also be effectively managed through treatment with TAE, further supporting their findings.
Notably, in our case, TAE not only reduced the size of
the embolized tumor but also that of the non-embolized tumor. Although HCAs are known to spontaneously regress
upon discontinuation of oral contraceptives and androgenic
steroids, this is unlikely to have been the cause in our case,
as no hormonal agents were used. Previous reports have indicated that CPSS-induced HCAs may be managed by surgical closure of the CPSS (11). In this case, it is possible that
the shrinkage of the HCAs following TAE was due to correction of excess compensatory arteries. Further case studies
are needed to confirm this hypothesis.
In conclusion, individuals with CdLS and CPSS can develop HCAs, and TAE may be an effective treatment approach in such cases.
